[0] JOEL BERGUM, CEO of Hornet Dev.
[3] I'm here today to talk about the unreasonable effectiveness of BM25 for Argentic Search.
[11] So how many of you have heard about BM25 before?
[14] Is it new or is it?
[15] Well, quite a few, so that's great.
[17] I'm also watching the World Cup.
[20] Norway is playing there against Ivory Coast's second half.
[24] Norway is leading, so that's good.
[26] So yeah, and at Hornet we are building retrieval infrastructure
[31] for agents.
[32] And I've been working on search and retrieval problems
[36] for a long time.
[37] As you can tell, I'm gray-haired.
[40] Been working in this space for more than 20 years.
[45] And in the talk today, I'll talk about why
[47] this kind of 30-year-old lexical scoring function
[51] is making a strong comeback.
[55] First, I will talk a little bit about what
[57] I mean by Argentic Search or Argentic Attribute
[59] and kind of define that for all of you.
[64] My definition is that Argentic Search is essentially
[67] searched inside agent loop.
[70] So you have an agent that is trying to accomplish a task,
[73] write the coding, or do some deep research, or whatever task.
[78] And inside that, you have some kind of information need
[81] for the agent in order to get that task done successfully.
[85] And you essentially need three things to kind of build a good
[90] Argentic Search system.
[92] And that is you need a capable model, a model that is able to
[96] use tools and is able to formulate queries.
[100] You also need a harness around the model and how you kind of
[104] expose the retrieval and the search functions to the model.
[108] There's different ways to do that.
[110] It could be through tool calling, or it could be through code
[113] mode.
[114] Ido here demonstrated what I call code mode for exposing
[119] retrieval infrastructure.
[121] So that's the harness part.
[122] And then you also need a retrieval engine to be able to do
[128] searches efficiently, potentially over a billion scaled document
[133] sets.
[133] And to define BM25, BM25 actually stands for best match 25.
[141] So there were some researchers doing plenty of different
[143] experiments.
[144] And experiment number 25 turned out to be the best one.
[148] So that's the background of the name.
[151] It's essentially a scoring function.
[153] So you can imagine you have a query, and you have a document,
[156] and you calculate some kind of score by interaction between the
[160] query terms and the document terms.
[162] And you come up with a score, and you hope that this score is a good
[166] proxy for the relevancy of the document with regards to the query.
[170] So one way to calculate BM25 would be to take all the documents and
[175] score each of them, and then figure out what are the top K documents.
[180] And then there's like 30 or 40 years of interest in how you accelerate
[185] that type of retrieval, top K, lots of different algorithms.
[189] We also invest a lot in that.
[190] I'll show something in this direction.
[193] But BM25 is the scoring function.
[195] And there is a way to kind of accelerate top K retrieval.
[200] BM25 hasn't changed.
[203] It's the same scoring function.
[205] But the change here is really that we got a more powerful user.
[209] Edo talked about general knowledge.
[212] The LLMs today have a lot of general knowledge.
[214] They know about entities.
[216] They know about companies.
[217] They know about dates.
[218] They know a lot.
[220] And by using that kind of implicit knowledge that is built into the
[224] parametric model, they essentially become very good at search.
[230] And that's the really change here now that is kind of making BM25
[235] more relevant.
[237] And BM25 used to be a kind of a baseline function.
[241] Any information retrieval research would include a BM25 baseline.
[245] And then you would put something fancy, advanced, neural, fancy stuff.
[250] And then you would compare it with BM25.
[253] And I also think it's interesting in how we evaluate search before.
[256] Because you will simply look at 10 blue links.
[259] And you scan it.
[260] And you compute some metrics.
[262] A lot of that is now going away because the agent is not really
[267] it's kind of powerful in the way that it can type out a lot more
[272] queries than a human can do.
[273] So it's less relevant to think about evaluating these systems just
[277] by a single shot query.
[281] And this is one of my favorite benchmarks out there.
[286] I like to talk about benchmarks.
[287] So BrowseCom Plus is a deep research benchmark published
[293] in a paper last year.
[295] And it has almost exactly 830 questions.
[302] These are riddle-like.
[303] Think about it like a pub quiz.
[305] Do you have pub quizzes in the US?
[307] Yeah, OK, great.
[308] So like kind of a riddle type of questions, quite long.
[312] And the agent, the harness of this kind of protocol
[316] of this benchmark is that you have a model.
[319] And it gets a very simple tool called search.
[323] And it accepts a query string.
[324] And you return some snippets back to the model.
[328] And the corpus is about 100,000 documents.
[332] So that's kind of tiny.
[333] And these are web documents.
[336] And the end-to-end accuracy, all of these questions
[339] have a golden reference answer.
[341] And you can kind of check if the model and the entire loop
[344] produces that exact answer.
[350] But why do we need retrieval?
[354] I like to compare context windows with floppy disks,
[358] because I'm old in the 80s.
[359] We installed these kind of games on our computers
[362] using floppy disks.
[363] So one kind of you guys are so young,
[366] so you don't probably have this kind of nostalgia.
[368] But one floppy disk could fit about 1.4 megabytes of data.
[374] And the current models, before they start degrading in quality,
[379] that's, in my opinion, around 350,000 tokens.
[383] So that's one floppy disk of data.
[386] So you need retrieval in order to fetch the information
[391] that you actually need to put into the context window.
[395] And BrowseCom Plus really demonstrate how retrieval quality
[402] affects the end-to-end accuracy of the task.
[405] The end-to-end accuracy here is essentially,
[407] is the model equipped with this search tool
[411] able to answer the question, the riddle-like question?
[415] And if you artificially just stuff the evidence documents that
[421] is needed to answer this question into the context window
[425] of the model, the accuracy is really high.
[429] So reasoning is not the bottleneck.
[431] The model, given the evidence up front,
[435] answers the question with a very high accuracy rate, even GPT-4.
[441] But if you expose the model with the harness with the retrieval tool,
[445] that accuracy falls, because it now depends on the harness,
[449] it depends on the model's ability to formulate queries,
[453] and the retrieval quality of the retriever.
[457] So for me, this is also quite important,
[460] because even if we get perfect models,
[463] like models that are kind of AGI,
[465] you don't have to append, make no mistakes,
[468] you still will be limited to a context window that
[471] is approximately a floppy disk, right?
[472] So you have to decide what goes into that context window.
[476] And I think retrieval is still very relevant,
[478] as the previous slide showed.
[482] And in this Browse Comp Plus dataset,
[485] one of these riddle-like questions
[487] become a search trajectory, because the model
[490] executes the query, gets some response back, reads it,
[494] reformulates the query, and continues until it has kind of filled up
[498] the context window, or found the answer, whatever comes first.
[505] And we spent some time to investigate these trajectories,
[512] to see how GPT-5 is formulating queries.
[517] And we found a lot of interesting aspects with that.
[521] We described it in a recent blog post, as well.
[523] You can find it on Hornet.deb.
[526] And we like to compare it with AOL query logs.
[530] So AOL was like a service back in the day,
[534] had some search interface.
[536] And they accidentally published a very large sample of what
[542] people were searching for on the web.
[545] And they were quite short.
[547] And I have seen more recent query logs, as well.
[550] And the user human pattern are still searching with just a few terms.
[556] GPT-5, on the other hand, it's a much more powerful user.
[559] It has the general knowledge.
[560] And it can, bam, write out very long queries.
[563] It can use a lot of syntax operators that are useful.
[569] It has learned from web search, or site operator, phrases, et cetera.
[573] And this is a new type of workload.
[579] And on BM25.
[582] BM25 has essentially two hyperparameters that controls various
[587] aspects of the scoring function.
[589] And I talked about having a baseline.
[592] And BM25 is usually a baseline.
[594] And BrowseCompPlus, as well, has a baseline with BM25.
[598] But it turns out that that baseline is terrible.
[602] So when you look at fancier techniques, embedding models,
[606] what have you, it stands out as a much better retrieval paradigm
[612] than BM25, if you look at the original paper.
[615] But more recent research shows that the parameters that
[619] were used in the BrowseCompPlus research paper
[622] was not really adequate to handle these kind of long documents.
[625] So I like this, which BM25 do you mean?
[629] Because it has a quite dramatic impact on that specific benchmarks
[633] on the overall accuracy.
[638] And why is BM25 now more powerful with the new user?
[644] So I mentioned the general knowledge of the user
[646] and that he can type faster and be more specific
[649] as a more powerful user.
[651] And exact matching is still relevant, right?
[654] Because the model knows names, entities, zip codes, SKUs,
[659] what have you.
[660] That is not so easy to represent with an embedding model,
[664] which kind of encodes all the tokens into a fixed vocabulary.
[669] It's also relatively cheap, especially if you take into consideration
[674] the cost of doing embedding inference.
[676] Some of these embedding models have like 8 billion parameters
[679] and you encode text and you have to stand up infrastructure for this
[682] and what have you.
[684] So it's quite simple.
[685] And also the tooling in the overall ecosystem is quite good.
[691] So it's readily available.
[694] And it's also very easy for the model to inspect the results
[697] and understand why a certain query formulation returned
[700] the result it did right.
[702] Because you're matching literal terms and phrases and things
[705] like that, which can help it kind of reformulate the queries.
[711] So these are the three key things.
[715] And now into more hot topics on what is all you need.
[720] And this is a very recent research that came out from Waterloo,
[724] from Jimmy Lin's group up there.
[725] They are doing a great job at the information retrieval research
[729] and also on agentic search.
[731] They have a recent paper that I love.
[734] It's called Scaling Direct Corpus Interaction
[737] Via Dynamic Workspace Expansion.
[740] So I'll spend some time on expanding this.
[743] So imagine you want to stand up web search infrastructure
[746] for agents.
[747] A lot of companies are doing that at the moment.
[750] We are also working with some of these companies
[753] to help them build infrastructure for powering
[755] that kind of use case.
[757] And there you have potentially billions of documents.
[761] So that doesn't fit into the context window.
[763] So you obviously need retrieval.
[765] And BM25 is a good baseline.
[767] So you can retrieve information over that.
[771] And the results of this is you can imagine this as a search engine
[779] result page, SERP, for agents.
[783] Because you can place these documents that are retrieved from
[787] the retriever into a workspace.
[789] And if you organize this workspace as a file system,
[793] you can play into the same things that you have around skills.
[797] You can have progressive disclosure.
[799] Because you can have the document, like the title of the document,
[803] and a small snippet of the document, and expose that to the model.
[807] And the model can then also decide, oh, I need to read more of the document.
[811] And when it's doing that, it can use all the primitive tools that it's really good at using.
[816] You all use coding agents.
[818] You all see in grep, and rip grep, and sed, and orc, and whatever it's doing to kind of manage context.
[824] So here you get the benefits of both worlds.
[826] And also you get to combine sandbox infrastructure, retrieval infrastructure, and VFS, and just bash,
[832] and whatever.
[833] So it's also quite exciting, right?
[835] Because it combines all of these new type of paradigms that is happening at the moment.
[839] So I'm really excited about this type of direction.
[842] And it's also kind of a hack to optimize for what the models are good at at the moment,
[848] because all the frontier LLM companies are optimizing their model for coding,
[852] for bash, for tool use.
[855] So if you put your kind of end-to-end task on the trajectory of that,
[859] you kind of, whatever, there's a new model,
[861] you know there's going to be better at this as well, right?
[865] So it might be that when we get AGI, they can just use the browser, we'll see.
[870] But currently this is a very powerful way to build retrieval infrastructure,
[875] and a whole editing search experience.
[881] And when it comes to evaluation, right, I talked about this earlier as well,
[885] in traditional information retrieval we were used to having just one query,
[890] one rank list, compute and DGD, and compare it.
[895] That is no longer very relevant when the new user is an agent,
[898] because that agent can reformulate queries, and do more queries,
[902] and do expansion, and do all kinds of different stuff.
[905] So a lot of the classical information retrieval evaluation
[909] is now kind of dead.
[911] Instead, look at, like, see if the model can perform the task it's set to.
[917] And for example, for question answering,
[919] does it get the answer right?
[920] And we, at Hornet, we are betting on BM25 as one of the primitives.
[928] And we have set out on the vision to kind of have the best, most efficient way
[934] to evaluate BM25, because I think it's such a strong fundamental primitive.
[941] And this illustration compares some anonymized engines, comparing with Hornet,
[947] on the same type of hardware, with web documents, 100 million web documents,
[954] on a single node.
[956] And as you can see, Hornet has a much more efficient implementation than the other engines,
[961] and can do more throughput for the same type of box, which, for a lot of companies that
[967] are building infrastructure at the moment for web search, et cetera, means a lot in savings.
[972] What is the y-axis?
[974] The y-axis is QPS.
[977] Sorry.
[978] The y-axis is, oh, sorry.
[982] The y-axis is latency.
[984] I'm sorry.
[985] So, four claims to take away from this talk.
[992] There's a new user.
[994] It's more powerful.
[997] It's able to type faster.
[999] It's able to read faster.
[1001] It's able to reformulate queries.
[1003] And it has a lot of general knowledge, which makes simple tools like grep and BM25 more powerful.
[1009] That's number one.
[1012] Number two, which BM25 do you mean?
[1016] There are differences in implementation, in performance, in parameters.
[1020] So think about that.
[1022] And also, why is it effective for agentic search?
[1025] It's simply because it's explainable for the model.
[1028] So the model can see and also use it in combination with grep, right?
[1032] Because you have literal matches, and grep is almost about literal matches as well.
[1037] And the combination of these two is a very strong agentic search or agentic retrieval paradigm.
[1047] There's a lot of references.
[1048] I think I will publish a talk.
[1051] Or the talk will be published, and also the slides.
[1055] And if you hated it, you can tweet at me.
[1064] I was told that there's not a room for questions.
[1066] But happy to chat about retrieval.
[1069] You will find me around the conference.
[1071] Probably the best way to reach me is through my X account.
[1076] And that's it.
